newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urges Peru and Ecuador to avoid arms race.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges Peru and Ecuador to avoid arms race.

text.p: The United States on Thursday urged Peru and Ecuador to avoid an arms race in their border dispute, after Peru bought 12 MiG-29 fighter planes from Belarus.

The U.S. State Department said Washington was disappointed by the Peruvian purchase of a squadron of MiG-29s from the former Soviet state and urged the two Andean countries to settle an old border conflict peacefully.

"We strongly urge both countries, Peru and Ecuador, to maintain their pledge of October 6, 1995 ... to avoid the risks of an arms race so as not to undermine the end of hostilities or otherwise damage the peace," spokesman Glyn Davies said.
The United States is a guarantor of a 1942 treaty under which Peru and Ecuador are trying to solve by diplomatic means their dispute over the Cordillera del Condor territory.
Skirmishes have occurred between the two Andean neighbours almost every year since that pact was signed, but in early 1995 the fighting grew into a brief, full-fledged war.

With the help of the United States, Argentina, Brazil and Chile, the governments of Lima and Quito reached a ceasefire agreement last year. Last month they also agreed to start talks in December on substantive issues of their dispute.
But the purchase of the most sophisticated jet fighters in the region could undermine talks and was denounced by Ecuador.

"The purchase of such a big number of combat planes and the level of their technical sophistication greatly exceeds Peru's declared intentions and would signify the start of an arms race there," Ecuador's Foreign Ministry statement said.

The Peruvian government said it was only replacing obsolete aircraft with the MiG-29s. It said some of the old jets had been irreparably damaged in last year's month-long war with Ecuador in January 1995.

Earlier this year Ecuador acquired four Israeli K-fir fighter-bombers for $13 million, sparking protests by Peru. That deal had required a U.S. license because the jets contained U.S.-made components.
